Exceptions to the rules
Credit hasn't blinkedHY spreads near record tights while the Fed hikes into 40.54× CAPE. Credit is either right (no recession) or the last to know — no middle ground at these spreads. Confirm: Spreads stay contained through the next hike. · Refute: Credit proxy breaks >2.5% below its 50-day average.
Narrow leadership, complacent volMag7 correcting while the index holds and VIX sleeps — distribution-phase behavior wearing an expansion-phase mask. Confirm: Mag7 gap narrows below 5 pts (breadth healing). · Refute: Gap widens past 12 pts (rollover risk).
The long end is doing the tightening10Y at 5.29% vs funds at 3.75–4.00% prices fiscal risk, not just Fed policy — a term-premium revolt, not a normal hiking cycle. Confirm: 10Y rolls over on soft CPI. · Refute: 10Y prints new highs into further hikes.
Historical analogs
1999–2000 — closest rhymeCAPE ~44 then vs 40.54 now; narrow must-own leadership; Fed hiking into strength; credit calm until it wasn't. Confirm: Credit widens while the index holds. · Refute: Breadth heals and the Fed pauses.
2018 Q4 — the mechanism to fearHiking on autopilot into rich valuations; −20% in a quarter; credit serene weeks earlier. Confirm: Hawkish surprise plus vol spike. · Refute: Fed signals pause.
1994–95 — comforting, likely wrongAggressive hikes and bond pain, but CAPE was 24× and the hikes actually slowed the economy — transmission worked. This cycle's broken transmission cuts both ways. Confirm: Economy absorbs hikes; 1995-style rip follows. · Refute: Transmission was just lagged — the break arrives late.

What happened
Sep 16 FOMC Decision + SEP decided

Outcome Raised the federal funds target range 25bp to 3.75–4.00%, unanimous 12-0 vote — the Fed's first rate hike in three years. New SEP median points to 4.1% at end of 2026 and 2027, with the longer-run rate at 3.2%.

Market reaction Widely anticipated (markets had ~83–85% odds of the hike priced going in); the unanimity was the surprise. Markets repriced toward one more 25bp hike in December.

Oct 14 CPI Sep 2026 decided

Outcome September CPI printed hot (BLS, Oct 14, 8:30 AM ET): headline +0.6% m/m, 3.7% y/y; core +0.3% m/m, 2.6% y/y — core a tenth above the +0.2% consensus anchor, with gasoline (+9.1% m/m) driving over half the headline increase.

Market reaction The 10-year spiked ~9bp intraday to ~5.31% but closed Oct 14 at 5.19% — inside the 5.2–5.5% containment band, not a falsifier trip. October hike odds repriced from ~22% to roughly 40% for the Oct 27–28 FOMC. Bank credit did not crack on the print (BAC's drop was a $1.2B Treasury settlement charge, not provisions).

Oct 28 FOMC Decision Oct 27-28 decided

Outcome Held the federal funds target range at 3.75–4.00% on a 10-2 vote — Hammack and Cook dissented in favor of a 25bp hike. Statement: inflation remains elevated relative to 2%; activity expanding at a solid pace. IORB unchanged at 3.90%.

Market reaction Muted: S&P 500 +0.28% to 7,743.98, VIX 16.91, 10Y 5.05%. Two hawkish dissents kept December live — CME FedWatch priced ~83% odds of a 25bp December hike after the decision. Minutes due Nov 18.

Nov 3 VOTE US Midterm Elections decided

Outcome Democrats won control of both chambers (AP calls): the Senate flipped from a 53-47 Republican majority, and the House flipped with Hakeem Jeffries in line for Speaker. Result is divided government for the last two years of the Trump term; no veto-proof majority.

Market reaction Clean, uncontested outcome — the post-midterm base rate (gridlock continuity) applies. S&P 500 +1.58% on Nov 4 to 7,688.62 and VIX fell 20.83 → 16.61; the relief did not hold — the index dropped 4.36% the next day on the AI-capex selloff, unrelated to the vote.

Nov 6 JOBS NFP Oct 2026 decided

Outcome October payrolls +165K vs ~65K consensus; unemployment 4.1% (vs 4.2% expected); average hourly earnings +0.4% m/m, +3.1% y/y; participation 61.9%. August–September revised up a combined 84K. Soft spots: U-6 rose to 7.9% from 7.6%; part-time jobs +339K.

Market reaction Hawkish: 10Y +3bp to ~4.87%, 2Y +6bp to ~4.53%, dollar index +0.7%; December hike odds rose to ~78% from 70% (LSEG). Equities bounced anyway after Thursday's rout — S&P 500 +0.31% to 7,376.86, Nasdaq +1.1% — but the S&P lost 2.7% on the week.

Nov 10 CPI Oct 2026 decided

Outcome October CPI +0.4% m/m vs +0.3% consensus (September +0.6%); core +0.3% m/m vs +0.2% consensus (second straight 0.3%). No 12-month rate published — BLS has no October 2025 baseline after the 2025 shutdown. Shelter +0.3% (>30% of the headline gain); energy +0.7% (gasoline +1.0%, electricity +0.9%); food +0.5%; transportation services +0.8%; used cars -1.2%.

Market reaction Hawkish: CME FedWatch fully priced a 25bp December hike and 50bp odds rose to ~14% from ~0. S&P 500 -0.38% to 7,520.93 (off an intraday low near -0.7%); VIX 19.92 to 19.46; MOVE 85.98 to 92.43; DXY +0.6% to 102.23. Equities recovered next session: S&P +1.31% to 7,619.38 on Nov 11, VIX 17.49.

Fed funds 3.75–4.00% (Sep 16 hike; down from the 5.14% 2024 peak) · HY spreads ~278bps, near the tightest in the post-1997 record · CAPE 40.54×, second-highest since 1881 · SPX 7,562 (Nov 13, 2026 close). The period to compare against is 1994–95 — the last time the Fed tightened aggressively while equities kept climbing (rates 4.2%→5.8%, SPX +34%, spreads calm). Key difference: CAPE was ~24× then vs 40.54× now. A slower-tightening alternative: 2015–19 (rates 0.1%→2.2%, SPX +58%, CAPE 24×→30×).

Pattern emerging

Rate cuts without a credit scare. The Fed cut from 5.14% to ~3.5% through mid-2026, then hiked to 3.75–4.00% on Sep 16, while HY spreads stayed near record tights and equities pushed to record valuation. The 2001 and 2008 cutting cycles arrived with spreads peaking near 912bps and 1,725bps — this cycle never widened. What to watch: HY OAS widening past ~400–600bps, M2 growth stalling from +4.6%, or SPX losing its 200-day. This is an analog, not a prediction — at 40.54× CAPE the margin for error is thin.

Long-Horizon Valuation · Three Models · 2026–2030

S&P 500 — Long-Horizon Valuation Fans (2026–2030)

Three independent models — EPS × P/E, CAPE reversion, and institutional — each drawn as a band from its bear to its bull scenario. The band is the honest part: one line to the moon would be a lie.

Context only: these fans frame long-horizon (2026–2030) valuation scenarios. They are not a near-term forecast and not a trading signal.

Where today sits: S&P 500 $7,562 at the 2026-11-13 close — 3.61% below its 120-day high ($7,845) and 3.02% above its 200-day ($7,340). The fan starts here: every model path begins at today's level, so the current price is the fan's origin — the fan answers where the level goes from here, not where it sits inside a range.

How to read this chart: one model at a time — pick a model above. Its bottom edge = bear scenario, its top edge = bull scenario, its center line = the scenario selected below. The table underneath compares all three models at 2030, so you can see where they agree and where they don't.
Model 1 · EPS × P/E

Uses: FactSet EPS trajectory × Goldman P/E path. Gives: year-end S&P 500 price.

Model 2 · CAPE reversion

Uses: current CAPE 40.54× pulled toward its long-run average at a chosen speed + EPS growth. Gives: implied price level.

Model 3 · Institutional

Uses: Vanguard / Research Affiliates / GMO annualized return forecasts. Gives: price range from compounding today's level.

Model comparison — 2030 S&P 500 implied price

Methodology transparency: Model 1 uses FactSet/Goldman EPS consensus × P/E — a structured calculation, not an analyst price target. Model 2 applies CAPE mean-reversion to current CAPE 40.54× with EPS growth — mathematically grounded valuation headwind. Model 3 translates Vanguard VCMM Mar 2026, Research Affiliates Jan 2026, GMO Q1 2026 10-year return forecasts into price levels. Each model is drawn as a band across its bear/base/bull scenarios — the spread between the edges is genuine uncertainty, not decoration. Rate path is context only.
